newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China policy guru Lu Ping speaks, Hong Kong listens.
newsitem.headline: China policy guru Lu Ping speaks, Hong Kong listens.

text.p: In the early 1990s he roared, and the Hong Kong stock market plunged.
Share traders are now immune to outbursts from Lu Ping, China's Hong Kong policy-maker, but he is no less influential.
Lu, the director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, has been a powerful figure in the territory's often rocky journey back to China's control at midnight on June 30.
That moment marks the end of 156 years of colonial rule. Britain seized Hong Kong from China's Qing dynasty in the 19th century after winning the war over the opium trade.

The territory's stock market used to push the panic button whenever Lu blasted the colonial administration, for example on the financing of a new international airport and container terminal, or on Governor Chris Patten's democratic reforms.
After a while, the markets eventually ignored his blasts. China and Britain also agreed on the financing of two of Hong Kong's major infrastructure projects.

But when he vanished from the limelight for six months in 1995, this territory of 6.4 million again grew jittery, with rife speculation that he was dying of cancer and that instability would set in if he were replaced.

Lu, 69, born in the western Chinese province of Sichuan, the home region of the late Chinese patriarch and architect of the Hong Kong handover, Deng Xiaoping, joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1945.
He graduated in 1947 from St John's University, an elitist tertiary institution of old Shanghai which provided China with some top bureaucrats, diplomats, doctors, scientists and entrepreneurs.

Alumni from the university where the rich and famous sent their children for higher education included Chinese Vice President Rong Yiren, internationally renowned architect I.M. Pei and banker Jing Shuping.
The prestige university, set up in 1879, was closed three years after the Communists took power in 1949.
Lu speaks many languages and is viewed by analysts as a man with a sharp, sophisticated mind.

He was promoted to be director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office in 1990 after spending three years as deputy director. He was a key figure in the drafting of the Basic Law, Hong Kong's post-handover constitution.
He is said to be a trusted confidant of Chinese Premier Li Peng, who frequently summons Lu to the Communist Party leadership compound at Zhongnanhai in Beijing to seek advice on Hong Kong.
Whenever he visits the territory, he is a magnet for pro-democracy protesters voicing outrage against China's plan to roll back democracy and civil liberties.
China plans to disband the elected Legislative Council and replace it with a handpicked assembly on July 1.
Lu never meets the protesters head on.
He has a habit of leaving by side doors and back doors to dodge protests, exposing himself to ridicule.
During one such cat-and-mouse episode with protesters last year, his car ran over the foot of a policeman outside China's official mission in Hong Kong, the Xinhua News Agency.
Apart from protesters, he also avoids Patten, whom China has dubbed a "political whore" and "criminal for 10,000 years".
Lu stirred controversy when he said in a television interview last year that advocacy of independence for Taiwan and Tibet would not be allowed in Hong Kong after the handover.
